parameters.note: A hypothesis is 'ruled out' on the workbench board when its evidence-updated posterior falls below this probability at a stage end. A workbench display convention, not a clinical quantity; no consulted source defines it and it is never presented as one.

An anchoring event is recorded when a learner board assigns at least this probability to a hypothesis the workbench has already ruled out (posterior below rule_out_threshold) at the same or an earlier stage. Design/07 names anchoring's cognitive family (the diagnostic-error literature it cites attributes ~70-75% of errors partly to cognitive factors) but defines no numeric threshold; this one is a project convention, flagged as such.

An ordered test is 'discriminating' if its results (a) move the leading hypothesis's workbench posterior by at least this amount, or (b) move any hypothesis across the rule-out threshold, or (c) change the top-ranked hypothesis. A test that settles a guideline criterion block (met or unmet) without meeting (a)-(c) is 'criteria-completing'. A test whose role is excluding a must-not-miss hypothesis without a quantified LR is 'safety-net'. Anything else is 'non-contributory'. These are bookkeeping rules for the debrief, defined here so the checker can recompute them; they are not clinical claims.

Workbench posteriors are computed by multiplying cited likelihood ratios onto declared priors, one hypothesis at a time (each published LR is a for/against statement about its own target condition versus the alternatives in its source studies), then normalising. This assumes conditional independence of findings, which is false in general — Murphy's sign and RUQ tenderness are not independent — and the board is therefore a teaching instrument, not a probability estimate for a real patient. C3's own conclusion stands over the whole mechanism: no single finding rules cholecystitis in or out, and the computed board never overrides the guideline criteria blocks, which are evaluated separately and reported alongside.

sources.consulted: Criteria table (A: systemic inflammation — fever and/or shaking chills, laboratory evidence of inflammatory response: abnormal WBC count, increased serum CRP; B: cholestasis — jaundice with total bilirubin >= 2 mg/dL, abnormal liver function tests: ALP, GGT, AST, ALT elevated; C: imaging — biliary dilatation, evidence of the etiology such as stricture, stone, stent. sources.citation: Birindelli A, Sartelli M, Di Saverio S, et al. 2020 WSES guidelines for the detection and management of bile duct injury during cholecystectomy. World J Emerg Surg. 2021;16:30. DOI 10.1186/s13017-021-00369-w (PMC8190978)
sources.consulted: Consulted in full text in-session (PMC8190978), key questions 3, 4, 6, 7 and Table 2. Classification (Table 2): Strasberg A = cystic duct leak or leaks from small ducts in the liver bed; B = occlusion of an aberrant right hepatic duct; C = leak from an aberrant right hepatic duct; D = lateral injury to the CBD; E subdivided by the Bismuth level: CBD stump > 2 cm = Bismuth I / Strasberg E1; stump < 2 cm = II / E2; ceiling of the confluence intact = III / E3; ceiling destroyed = IV / E4; type I-III plus stricture of an isolated right duct = V / E5. Major BDIs (Strasberg E) are associated with tissue loss (e.g. the common bile duct is clipped and transected) and require Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy (KQ4 statement 4.2: hepaticojejunostomy is the treatment of choice for major BDIs). Presentation (KQ6 review): the two most frequent scenarios are bile leakage and bile duct obstruction; cholestatic jaundice with choluria, fecal acholia, and pruritus are the most common signs of the obstruction/stricture picture; in complete occlusion bilirubin rises; ALP and bilirubin are the early cholestasis markers. Investigations (statements 6.1-6.3): prompt investigation of alarm symptoms (fever, abdominal pain, distention, jaundice, nausea, vomiting); LFTs including bilirubin, AST, ALT, ALP, GGT; CT first-line for collections and ductal dilation, complemented by CE-MRCP for exact visualisation, localisation, and classification. MRCP is the 'gold standard' for complete morphological evaluation of the biliary tree, showing anatomy proximal and distal to the injury. ERCP limits: it does not visualise ducts upstream of an obstructing lesion, and endoscopic treatments for bile leaks are ineffective 'except in the case of transection of the common bile duct or common hepatic duct' (review text: endoscopic therapy cannot bridge a transection). Hepatobiliary scintigraphy is more sensitive and specific than US/CT for bile leaks but has poor spatial resolution and pitfalls in large duct defects. Postoperative management (statements 7.3-7.5): major BDI (E1-E2) diagnosed within 72 h — referral to an HPB-expert centre if expertise is unavailable locally, urgent Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy may follow; diagnosed between 72 h and 3 weeks — percutaneous drainage of fluid collections whenever present, targeted antibiotics, nutritional support, PTBD may be useful for septic patients with complete CBD obstruction, and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy after a minimum of 3 weeks once the acute situation has resolved; late-presenting stricture — Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy. Antibiotics (KQ5 review): in biliary obstruction without bile leak or signs of sepsis, antibiotic therapy may not be required.

sources.citation: American Association of Electrodiagnostic Medicine (AAEM), with the American Academy of Neurology and the American Academy of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation. Practice parameter for electrodiagnostic studies in ulnar neuropathy at the elbow: summary statement. Neurology 1999;52:688-690; Muscle Nerve 1999;22 (summary statement PDF, aanem.org, consulted in full in-session 2026-11-06)
sources.consulted: The parameter's conclusions and recommendations as read: ulnar neuropathy at the elbow is a common peripheral mononeuropathy, second only to carpal tunnel syndrome in incidence. Its literature review rests on 13 qualifying articles (Class A evidence from 702 normal control elbows and 564 ulnar-neuropathy elbows): '13 articles reported sensitivities of electrodiagnostic studies ranging from 37% to 86% and specificities of 95% or greater.' Technique standards: surface stimulation and recording; elbow in moderate flexion (70 to 90 degrees); across-elbow distance of 10 cm; stimulation more than 3 cm distal to the medial epicondyle avoided. Focal-lesion criteria, listed in order of strength of evidence: (a) absolute motor nerve conduction velocity from above elbow to below elbow of less than 50 m/s; (b) an AE-to-BE segment greater than 10 m/s slower than the BE-to-wrist segment; (c) a decrease in CMAP negative peak amplitude from BE to AE greater than 20%, suggesting conduction block or temporal dispersion of focal demyelination; (d) a significant change in CMAP configuration at the AE site; multiple internally consistent abnormalities are more convincing than isolated ones. General principle: if ulnar studies are abnormal, further nerve conduction studies should be carried out to exclude a diffuse process (practice standard). Practice options when studies recording abductor digiti quinti are inconclusive: recording from the first dorsal interosseous, and an inching study over 1- or 2-cm increments. And when ulnar-innervated muscles are abnormal on needle examination, the examination should be extended to non-ulnar C8/medial cord/lower trunk muscles to exclude brachial plexopathy and to the cervical paraspinals to exclude radiculopathy. Case 5's stage-4 protocol is this document's protocol, and its electrodiagnostic LR is computed at the review's least favourable supported combination (0.37 sensitivity, 0.95 specificity) as a disclosed floor.

sources.citation: Chang KV, Wu WT, Han DS, Ozcakar L. Ulnar nerve cross-sectional area for the diagnosis of cubital tunnel syndrome: a meta-analysis of ultrasonographic measurements. Arch Phys Med Rehabil 2018;99(4):743-757 (PMID 28888384; PubMed abstract consulted in-session 2026-11-06)

sources.consulted: Consulted 2026-11-07 via the guideline's published text as reproduced in-session: chest pain described as sharp, fleeting, pleuritic (related to inspiration) or positional, or in shifting locations, suggests a lower likelihood of ischemia, and chest tenderness on palpation or pain with inspiration markedly reduces the likelihood of acute coronary syndrome; the guideline's physical-examination table assigns tenderness on the costochondral joints to costochondritis / Tietze syndrome, and lists palpation with pain reproducibility among the musculoskeletal examination findings. sources.citation: Proulx AM, Zryd TW. Costochondritis: Diagnosis and Treatment. Am Fam Physician. 2009;80(6):617-620.
sources.consulted: Consulted 2026-11-07 in full text in-session: costochondritis is an inflammation of the costochondral junctions of ribs or the chondrosternal joints of the anterior chest wall, usually at multiple levels and LACKING swelling or induration; palpation of the affected chondrosternal joints elicits tenderness, and pain is reproduced by palpation of the affected cartilage segments. It is usually self-limited and benign. Tietze syndrome, by contrast, is an inflammatory process causing VISIBLE ENLARGEMENT of the costochondral junction, usually at a single rib - the distinction case 7's Mondo refusal and its absent-swelling finding both turn on. Coronary artery disease is present in 3 to 6 percent of adult patients with chest pain and chest-wall tenderness to palpation. Patients older than 35 years, those with a history or risk of coronary artery disease, and any patient with cardiopulmonary symptoms should have an electrocardiogram and possibly a chest radiograph. Treatment as stated: acetaminophen or anti-inflammatory medications where safe and appropriate, avoidance of activities that produce chest muscle overuse, and reassurance.

sources.citation: Orloff LA, Wiseman SM, Bernet VJ, et al. American Thyroid Association Statement on Postoperative Hypoparathyroidism: Diagnosis, Prevention, and Management in Adults. Thyroid. 2018;28(7):830-841. doi:10.1089/thy.2017.0309
sources.consulted: Consulted 2026-11-07 in-session via the PubMed abstract and two full-text copies surfaced in-session (the publisher PDF fetch hit a verification wall; the text was read, not skimmed from snippets). Carries: hypoparathyroidism (hypoPT) after thyroid/parathyroid surgery results from parathyroid gland damage, devascularisation or removal; hypoPT is the most common complication of bilateral thyroid operations; the definition of postoperative hypoPT is a low intact PTH accompanied by hypocalcemia; biochemical hypoPT is a PTH below the lower limit of the laboratory standard (usually 12 pg/mL) together with hypocalcemia; hypocalcemia is a total serum calcium below 8.5 mg/dL; a postoperative PTH below 15 pg/mL marks increased risk of acute hypoPT, and a PTH of 15 pg/mL or above measured at least 20 minutes postoperatively in a patient whose serum calcium is in the normal range obviates the need for intensive monitoring or routine supplementation; supplementation is considered when PTH is below 15 pg/mL, calcium has declined below 8.5 mg/dL, or ionized calcium is below 1.1 mmol/L; the oral regimen is 400-1200 mg/day of elemental calcium (1-3 g/day calcium carbonate) in divided doses; calcitriol 0.25-0.5 micrograms twice daily is added for symptomatic hypocalcemia with serum calcium declining on sequential measurements or remaining below 7 mg/dL; patients on supplementation are monitored with serial calcium levels for rebound hypercalcemia; vitamin D and magnesium levels are monitored; transient hypoPT resolves within 6 months and disease beyond 6 months is chronic/permanent; preoperative vitamin D below 20 ng/mL (with low calcium and high alkaline phosphatase) relates to greater risk.

sources.citation: Fong J, Khan A. Hypocalcemia: updates in diagnosis and management for primary care. Can Fam Physician. 2012;58(2):158-162 (PMC3279267)
sources.consulted: Consulted 2026-11-07 in-session in full text. Carries: hypocalcemia is defined as a corrected total serum calcium below 2.12 mmol/L; roughly half of serum calcium is protein-bound, so the level must be corrected for albumin; hypoparathyroidism shows hypocalcemia with a low or inappropriately normal PTH and HYPERPHOSPHATEMIA, and is most commonly seen after total thyroidectomy (permanent hypoparathyroidism 0.5-6%); Box 1 lists hypomagnesemia and vitamin D inadequacy among the causes of hypocalcemia; the presenting tetany picture is paresthesia, circumoral numbness, muscle cramps and tetany, with prolonged QT interval among the associated findings; Trousseau's sign (carpopedal spasm after a blood-pressure cuff held above systolic for 3 minutes) is the more reliable sign, present in 94% of hypocalcemic individuals and only 1% to 4% of healthy people; Box 2 basic investigations are corrected calcium, phosphate, magnesium, electrolytes, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, pH and CBC, with ionized calcium among the further investigations; intravenous calcium is indicated when the total calcium is below 1.9 mmol/L, the ionized calcium is below 1 mmol/L, or the patient is symptomatic -- 1-2 10-mL ampoules of 10% calcium gluconate in 50-100 mL of 5% dextrose over 5-10 minutes, with cardiac monitoring during IV calcium necessary -- followed by oral calcium and calcitriol 0.25-1 micrograms/day as needed, correcting magnesium deficiency or alkalosis if present; chronic oral elemental calcium is 1-2 g three times daily (start 500-1000 mg three times daily); vitamin D inadequacy is 25(OH)D below 75 nmol/L.

sources.citation: Cooper MS, Gittoes NJ. Diagnosis and management of hypocalcaemia. BMJ. 2008;336(7656):1298-1302. doi:10.1136/bmj.39582.589433.BE (PMC2413335)
sources.consulted: Consulted 2026-11-07 in-session via the PMC full-text copies surfaced in-session.
